figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Performance of OpenVLHarness across models and settings. (a) Average score over 22 challenging multimodal benchmarks with and without OpenVLHarness, across the Qwen, Kimi, and GPT model families. (b) Benchmark scores for GPT-6 Luna and GPT-6 Astra at medium reasoning effort, each with and without OpenVLHarness; radii are rescaled per benchmark, and numbers give the raw scores of GPT-6 Astra (medium) with OpenVLHarness. (c) Average score versus model-token cost (average for 1,000 query rollouts) on 22 benchmarks for GPT-6 Luna alone and with Codex, Visual Sketchpad, or OpenVLHarness, across all five reasoning-effort settings.
figures.headline: Average scores rise with OpenVLHarness across Qwen, Kimi, and GPT model families on 22 challenging benchmarks.
citing_sentences: 1c) reveals diminishing returns at higher reasoning budgets: moving the base model from xhigh to max effort multiplies its model-token spending by 2.7 but improves its average score by only 0.7 points.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of OpenVLHarness. The MLLM orchestrator invokes capabilities through typed interfaces. The capability layer connects these interfaces to underlying models and services and renders their outputs into model-facing evidence: here, a labeled mask overlay accompanied by a textual description and normalized bounding boxes. Persistent multimodal memory retains image artifacts, structured data, and web references under reusable handles. An Environment Update advertises the available artifacts to the orchestrator, allowing subsequent calls to reuse earlier evidence, including through memory-grounded computation.
figures.headline: Diagram shows the orchestrator reusing grounding overlays, bounding boxes, and retained masks through memory handles in later calls.
citing_sentences: OpenVLHarness augments an MLLM orchestrator with two complementary mechanisms (Figure 2).
Figure 2 illustrates grounding for “cabinet” in input_image_3.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Qualitative examples of OpenVLHarness. (a) Camera poses, depth, and grounding are combined in code to measure a 3D distance (Example F). (b) Grounded crops are passed to OCR and image search, and the answer is verified on the web (Example F). (c) Masks from two grounding queries are reconciled in code to reach the exact count (Example F).
figures.headline: Three trajectories show code combining tool outputs to measure a distance in three dimensions, verify an answer on the web, and reach an exact count.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 shows three trajectories from our evaluation.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Failure diagnosis and harness specialization with Qwen3-VL-8B. We critique failure trajectories using Kimi K3. (a) Distribution of failure causes across four domains. (b) Proposed remedies: grouped into creating task-specific tools (A–C), updating harness text (Y), and no proposed remedy (Z). (c) Four datasets selected for contrasting remedy profiles: Y (orange) dominates ERQA and RealWorldQA, while A–C (blue) dominates SparBench and FREAK-VQA. (d) Gains from harness search and tool generation over the unoptimized harness. Harness search is more effective on datasets dominated by text-level changes, while tool generation yields larger gains when task-specific tools are preferred.
figures.headline: Harness search helps ERQA and RealWorldQA more, while tool generation helps SparBench and FREAK-VQA more.
citing_sentences: 4c): harness text changes (Y) dominate ERQA ($71\%$) and RealWorldQA ($56\%$), whereas task-specific tools (A+B+C) dominate SparBench ($75\%$) and FREAK-VQA ($62\%$).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Tool-call volume and engagement by domain. (a) Tool calls per question, averaged over all questions in the domain. (b) Fraction of questions answered with no tool call. Engagement varies with model scale within a family and not across families, and call volume does not order the models by accuracy.
figures.headline: Smaller models leave more questions without tool calls, and call volume does not order models by accuracy.
citing_sentences: Table 4 reports them per model, and Figure 5 resolves them by domain.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Distribution of tool calls across capabilities. All calls issued by each model, normalized to 100%. Visual Grounding is the largest consumer for every model; the models differ mainly in the second-ranked capability.
figures.headline: Visual Grounding takes the largest share of tool calls for every model, while the second-ranked capability differs across models.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Distribution of tool calls by domain. Calls issued in each domain as a share of that domain’s calls, with the call total below each panel. Colors are consistent across panels. Grounded perception is dominated by Visual Grounding for every model except GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra; visual search and deep research is the only domain dominated by the web capabilities; spatial reasoning is the only domain in which four capabilities carry comparable load.
figures.headline: Visual Grounding dominates grounded perception calls for most models, while web capabilities dominate visual search and deep research.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 resolves the same budget by domain.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Per-capability paired comparison against the base model. For each capability and model, the accuracy of OpenVLHarness minus that of the base model on the questions whose rollout invoked that capability. The corresponding difference on the questions that did not invoke it, which serves as the control, is given in the last column of Table 6 together with the share of questions each capability was invoked on.
figures.headline: Image Search improves accuracy by 18.9 to 27.1 points on questions that invoked it, well above its control values.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 reports, for each capability and model, the paired difference on the questions that invoked it.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Object-count distribution across counting benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Widely used benchmarks such as TallyQA, CountBenchQA, and PixmoCount are dominated by low counts: nearly all of their samples contain ten or fewer objects (and a majority of TallyQA fall in the $0$–$1$ bucket), capping at $10$–$15$. Only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS contain substantial mass in the high-count regime ($>50$ objects), reaching into the hundreds or thousands. This skew means accuracy on standard counting benchmarks largely reflects performance on small object counts and reveals little about high-count visual measurement.
figures.headline: Most counting benchmarks are dominated by low object counts, and only FSC-147 and FSCD-LVIS reach high-count regimes.
citing_sentences: To make this concrete, we bin every sample of widely used counting and grounding datasets by its number of target objects (Figures 9 and 10).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Object-count distribution across grounding benchmarks. Each bar shows the percentage of samples falling into binned object-count buckets, with the per-dataset maximum count annotated above. Referring-expression benchmarks such as RefCOCO/+/g and Ref-L4/GroundingME ground a single target per sample ($100\%$ in the $0$–$1$ bucket, $\text{max}=1$), and even detection-style sets like OdinW-13 ($97\%$) and LVIS ($86\%$) are overwhelmingly concentrated at one object per image. Only the FSCD variants exercise dense, many-object grounding. As with counting, this distribution implies that progress on common grounding benchmarks is measured almost entirely in the single- or few-object regime.
figures.headline: Most grounding benchmarks have one target per sample, and only the FSCD variants test dense, many-object grounding.
citing_sentences: To make this concrete, we bin every sample of widely used counting and grounding datasets by its number of target objects (Figures 9 and 10).

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7–12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7–8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

sections.body:
The paper argues that many visual questions need evidence the model cannot infer from the input alone, such as small objects, long-tail entities, or computed quantities. In the inference-time scaling study (Fig. 1c), moving the base model from xhigh to max effort multiplies its model-token spending by 2.7 but improves its average score by only 0.7 points.

OpenVLHarness has two parts. The capability layer gives consistent access to heterogeneous tools and renders their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory keeps images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts across turns. The evaluation covers 22 benchmarks and eight backbones, with average gains of 9.7–12.6 percentage points over base models.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Extra reasoning budget gives diminishing returns, so the paper proposes OpenVLHarness to add multimodal evidence acquisition.

sections.body:
Each capability is wrapped in a task-level interface, so a backend can change without changing the orchestrator's calls. For example, Visual Grounding can use SAM 3 or Grounding DINO. Each capability has an output processor that returns a labeled overlay, a description, and bounding boxes, while the raw masks and arrays go to memory.

- Memory registers images, structured data, and web references under handles such as `input_image_3` and `webpage_url_1`.
- An Environment Update lists the available handles after each tool turn.
- The Python Coding Agent runs generated code over stored bindings, such as averaging depth within each detected region.

The base set has nine capabilities.
sections.heading: Harness Design
sections.headline: OpenVLHarness pairs a capability layer that renders tool outputs with persistent memory of handle-addressed artifacts.

sections.body:
The section evaluates 22 datasets in four domains: grounded perception, visual search and deep research, general VQA and hallucination, and spatial reasoning. In Table 1, Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 48.56 on CountQA with OpenVLHarness against 32.00 without tools. Qwen3-VL results are means of three runs.

A Kimi K3 critic labels the primary cause of failed Qwen3-VL-8B trajectories across the 22 benchmarks. Its labels agree with human annotations on 92% of 100 sampled failures. Harness search improves ERQA by +4.1 and RealWorldQA by +3.7, while tool generation improves SparBench by +8.2 and FREAK-VQA by +4.5. The critique covers only failed trajectories, so it guides optimization rather than predicting recoverable accuracy.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: OpenVLHarness raises Qwen3-VL-8B scores on 22 benchmarks, for example from 32.00 to 48.56 on a counting benchmark.

sections.body:
Early systems compile a question into a fixed program of vision tools, so the plan cannot change after tool results arrive. Later multi-turn frameworks interleave reasoning with visual feedback but depend on task-specific designs that need extensive training. Visual Sketchpad and OctoTools are training-free, with manually designed tool interfaces. Working-memory methods such as ReWOO, CodeAct, HuggingGPT, and LLMCompiler pass intermediate results by reference, mostly in text settings.

OpenVLHarness extends these ideas to the multimodal setting with a unified registry of typed artifacts for images, structured data, and web evidence.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior visual tool-use systems use fixed plans or task-specific frameworks, while this paper keeps multimodal artifacts addressable across turns.

sections.body:
The conclusion summarizes the design: a capability layer with task-level interfaces and evidence rendering, persistent multimodal memory, and a Python Coding Agent that computes over stored data. Evaluation on 22 benchmarks and eight backbones shows broad gains. Component ablations are reported as showing incremental benefits of the capability layer and memory.

Harness search and tool generation specialize the system on selected domains without updating underlying model weights. The harness, tools, evaluation protocols, and optimization workflows are released.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Released harness gives broad gains on 22 benchmarks and can specialize to domains without updating model weights.

sections.body:
The analysis covers every rollout of the OpenVLHarness runs behind Tables 1 and 7 across five base models, using exact rather than sampled counts. Table 4 gives calls per question, such as 1.43 for Qwen3-VL-8B and 2.59 for Qwen3-VL-32B, and the share of questions answered with no call, from 28.9% to 2.6%. Table 5 pairs each model against its base, with gains from +6.2 to +10.1 points. On questions with no tool call, the null control ranges from -1.8 to +1.8 points.

Per-capability effects are correlational, so each is reported with a control computed on rows that did not invoke the tool.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix reports tool-call volume, capability distribution, paired accuracy effects, and object-count distributions of benchmarks.
